verses.text: Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin;
that you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God.
For we have spent enough of our past time doing the desire of the Gentiles, and having walked in lewdness, lusts, drunken binges, orgies, carousings, and abominable idolatries.
They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming:
who will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.
For to this end the Good News was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed as men in the flesh, but live as to God in the spirit.
But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you.
But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice; that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.
For let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer, or a meddler in other men’s matters.
But if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter.
For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God. If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?
“If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?”
Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.

footnotes.content: Christ suffered in the flesh to free us from sin's grip—that's the anchor we lean on when our own flesh wars against us. When we arm ourselves with His mind, we trade the slave's fear for a child's trust; we stop punishing ourselves for being human and start letting His suffering do the work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of your time on earth—what a tender way to say it. Not 'your whole life,' but the remainder, which may be short or long. Peter is saying: stop spending those days on the appetites of men, and start spending them on what God actually wants. That's where the real living happens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's naming the old list—lewdness, drunken binges, orgies—not to shame us, but to mark the line we've already crossed. We've already spent enough time on those things. There's a relief in that; it's permission to stop.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your old crowd will think you're strange—they'll blaspheme you for it. That sting is real. But notice: their confusion is not your problem to fix. You've made a different choice, and they don't understand yet. Stay steady.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They will give account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. That's not our job—judgment belongs to Christ alone. We're freed from that weight, and so are they, though they don't know it yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the dead heard the Gospel—there's mercy in that mystery. They are judged as humans in the flesh (as they lived), yet they can live toward God in the spirit. This verse holds a tenderness we don't always dwell on; the Gospel reaches further than our understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The end of all things is near—Peter writes with urgency, and we still feel it. He doesn't ask us to panic; he asks us to think clearly, stay calm, and watch in prayer. When everything feels thin and close, that's when a sober mind is a gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Love covers a multitude of sins. Not by excusing them, but by drawing near anyway, by choosing to see the person beneath the fault. That's how the Lord loves us—not blind to our sin, but steadfast over it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Be hospitable without grumbling—that small phrase changes everything. Hospitality without grumbling means you're not keeping score, not sighing over the guest, not storing up grievance. That's Christ's kind of welcome.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each of you has received a gift. Not some—each. Not to keep or display, but to employ in serving one another. We're all stewards of grace in its many forms, and the whole body gets weaker when one person holds back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If anyone speaks, let it be as the very words of God. That's high ground—not 'as though' or 'as if,' but 'as'—meaning your words carry that weight when they serve. The strength we employ comes from God alone, so that all glory goes to Jesus. That's the shape of faithful speech and service.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't be astonished at the fiery trial—Peter is saying, this is not a stranger at your door. It's part of what it means to follow. You've been warned, prepared; this is the shape of faith in a world that doesn't welcome it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because you are partakers of Christ's sufferings, rejoice. Your trial is not punishment—it's the privilege of walking His path. One day you'll share in His glory with the same fullness; that day is worth every sting now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed. The world's scorn can't touch what God has already given you—His Spirit of glory rests on you. What they mean for shame, He means for honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't suffer as a murderer, thief, or meddler—Peter is drawing a sharp line. There's a difference between suffering for Christ and suffering for your own folly. Make sure your pain is the price of faithfulness, not the fruit of carelessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you suffer for being a Christian, don't be ashamed. Let the name itself be a crown—don't shrink from it or hide it. In that moment, glorify God by standing firm in who you are in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judgment begins with the household of God—meaning we're first, not last. If it's hard for us who know Him and are refined by trial, what hope do those have who reject His News? There's a sobering logic here that calls us to faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If it is hard for the righteous to be saved—he's quoting Proverbs, pressing the question home. The righteous are saved, yes, but through fire and trial. If that's the path for the faithful, what door is left open for those who turn away?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to Him as a faithful Creator. Readers today hear an echo in this: in our own trials—illness, loss, confusion—we can commit ourselves to the One who made us and knows every inch of our frames. He will not let us fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
